name: Remington IPL home device
lead: Remington sells home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal devices under its iLight line. IPL uses broad-spectrum light absorbed by melanin in the hair to heat and damage the follicle, and repeated sessions are needed because only follicles in the growth phase respond.[1]

Wikipedia cites Remington as stating that IPL and laser devices should be used only on light to medium skin tones and work best on darker hair; the article presents this as a manufacturer claim.[1] Remington Products itself is an American personal-care brand whose history runs from 1937 electric shavers to current ownership by Spectrum Brands.[2]
No clinical trials of this specific device were found.
infobox: Broad-spectrum pulsed light targeting hair melanin
Light to medium skin, darker hair (manufacturer)

paras: Light is absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and follicle, heating the structure that produces hair. Visible removal generally takes multiple sessions weeks apart.[1] Unlike lasers, IPL uses non-coherent light with filters to choose wavelengths.[1][3]

Evidence for IPL comes from clinic-grade systems. A 2006 study cited by Wikipedia reported about 67 percent hair reduction at six months, and a randomized trial cited on the laser hair removal page reported 52.7 percent reduction with IPL versus 69.2 percent with a diode laser at 12 months.[1][3] These studies did not test Remington devices.

Reported effects of light-based hair removal include redness, swelling, itching, burns and pigment changes; photosensitising medications and sunburned skin are listed as contraindications.[1][3] Manufacturer guidance limits use to lighter skin tones.[1]
No studies found for this device. Studies of clinic IPL systems are summarised above.[1][3]

card.summary: Remington's home IPL flasher: reduces hair over repeated sessions on light-to-medium skin, no device-specific trials.
card.note: Manufacturer limits use to light-to-medium skin tones.

quick.overview:
A consumer IPL device that flashes broad-spectrum light to damage hair follicles over multiple sessions.

Evidence for IPL exists for clinic systems; none was found for this specific device.
quick.mechanism: Melanin in the hair absorbs the light and heats the follicle; only growing hairs respond, so sessions are repeated.
quick.risks: Burns, redness and pigment changes are reported with light-based removal; the manufacturer limits use to lighter skin tones.
